claim: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
source: The ability to associate sensory stimuli with abstract classes is critical for survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of sensory-abstract associations for survival, presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Experimental studies have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations and flexible ones.
source: Such experiments have probed two kinds of associations between stimuli and categories: fixed associations (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Cromer et al., 2010) (in which, e.g., stimuli are either in category A or in category B), and flexible ones (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004; Roy et al., 2010; Reinert et al., 2021) (in which, e.g., stimuli are in category A in one context and category B in another).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies that have investigated these two types of associations.

claim: Activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables such as category and context.
source: A consistent finding in these experiments is that activity of single neurons in associative cortex develops selectivity to task-relevant abstract variables, such as category (Freedman et al., 2001; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Reinert et al., 2021) and context (White and Wise, 1999; Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies showing selectivity development.

claim: Neurons typically display selectivity to multiple abstract variables.
source: Neurons, however, typically display selectivity to multiple abstract variables (Rigotti et al., 2013), and those patterns of mixed selectivity are often hard to intepret (Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Hirokawa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies documenting mixed selectivity patterns.

claim: Neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables via negatively correlated responses.
source: Classical work indicates that neurons in visual cortex encode simple sensory variables (e.g., two opposite orientations) via negatively correlated responses (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Olshausen and Field, 2004): neurons that respond strongly to a given variable respond weakly to the other one, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical studies in visual cortex.

claim: Responses in visual cortex are symmetric, with about the same number of neurons responding strongly to one variable or the other.
source: Those responses, furthermore, are symmetric (DeAngelis and Uka, 2003): about the same number of neurons respond strongly to one variable, or the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work on visual cortex.

claim: Evidence for negatively correlated and symmetric responses has been reported in monkeys and mice prefrontal cortex.
source: Evidence in favour of this type of responses has been reported in monkeys (White and Wise, 1999; Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008) and mice (Reinert et al., 2021) prefrontal cortex (PFC).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies in PFC.

claim: Evidence for positively correlated responses has been reported in experiments from monkeys lateral intraparietal cortex.
source: However, evidence in favour of a different type of responses has been reported in a different set of experiments from monkeys lateral intraparietal (LIP) cortex (Fitzgerald et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work in LIP cortex.

claim: In LIP cortex, responses to categories A and B were found to be positively correlated.
source: In that case, responses to categories A and B were found to be positively correlated: neurons that learn to respond strongly to category A also respond strongly to category B, and neurons that learn to respond weakly to category A also respond weakly to category B.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental findings cited from Fitzgerald et al., 2013.

claim: In LIP cortex, responses were strongly asymmetric with almost all neurons displaying the strongest response to the same category.
source: Furthermore, responses were strongly asymmetric: almost all neurons displayed the strongest response to the same category (despite monkeys did not display behavioural biases towards one category or the other).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental findings cited from Fitzgerald et al., 2013.

claim: The model hypothesizes that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function.
source: To this end, we hypothesize that synaptic connectivity in neural circuits evolves by implementing gradient descent on an error function (Richards et al., 2019).
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the modeling work, with a citation to related work.

claim: Under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks.
source: A large body of work has demonstrated that, under gradient-descent plasticity, neural networks can achieve high performance on both simple and complex tasks (LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to work on neural network performance.

claim: Gradient-descent learning can be implemented in a biologically plausible way.
source: Recent studies have furthermore shown that gradient-descent learning can be implemented, at least approximately, in a biologically plausible way (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Whittington and Bogacz, 2017; Sacramento et al., 2018; Akrout et al., 2019; Payeur et al., 2021; Pogodin and Latham, 2020; Boopathy and Fiete, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies on biologically plausible learning.

claim: The model can capture experimental findings showing that neurons become selective to category and context after learning.
source: Via mathematical analysis and simulations, we show that the model can capture the experimental findings discussed above. In particular, after learning, neurons in the model become selective to category and, if present, context; this result is robust, and independent of the details of the circuit and the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis and simulations presented in the paper.

claim: Whether correlations after learning are positive or negative depends on circuit and task details.
source: On the other hand, whether correlations after learning are positive or negative, and whether population tuning to different categories is asymmetric or not, is not uniquely determined, but depends on details.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis showing parameter-dependent behavior of correlations.

claim: Activity measures are modulated by circuit details including activation function of single neurons, learning rates, and initial connectivity.
source: We determined how, in the model, activity measures are modulated by circuit details (activation function of single neurons, learning rates, initial connectivity) and task features (number of stimuli, and whether or not the associations are context dependent).
evidence: This claim is supported by the systematic analysis of parameter dependencies presented in the paper.

claim: Activity measures are modulated by task features including number of stimuli and whether associations are context dependent.
source: We determined how, in the model, activity measures are modulated by circuit details (activation function of single neurons, learning rates, initial connectivity) and task features (number of stimuli, and whether or not the associations are context dependent).
evidence: This claim is supported by the systematic analysis of task dependencies presented in the paper.

claim: Before learning, the category selectivity index is zero on average.
source: Before learning, the responses of single neurons to different stimuli are random and unstructured. Thus, responses to stimuli paired with category A are statistically indistinguishable from responses to stimuli paired with category B (Figure 2A). This makes the category selectivity index zero on average (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: After learning, within-category responses become more similar than across-category responses.
source: After learning, the responses of single neurons depend on category: within-category responses become more similar than across-category responses, resulting in two separate distributions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The category selectivity index for most neurons increases after learning.
source: As a consequence, the category selectivity index for most neuron increases; correspondingly, average selectivity increases from zero to positive values (Figure 2F), thus reproducing the behaviour observed in experimental studies (Freedman et al., 2001; Freedman and Assad, 2006; Reinert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2F and citations to experimental studies.

claim: The selectivity increase is a universal property observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of parameters.
source: We found that the selectivity increase is a universal property – it is observed in all circuit models that successfully learned the task, independent of the parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Before learning, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated.
source: As discussed above, before learning the responses of neurons in the intermediate layer are random and unstructured. Thus, activity in response to different stimuli is uncorrelated; this is illustrated in Figure 2C, where all non-diagonal entries of the correlation matrix are close to zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Before learning, the category correlation is close to zero.
source: Before learning, the category correlation is close to zero (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop structure with correlations becoming different within diagonal and off-diagonal blocks.
source: Over learning, the correlation matrices develop structure. Correlations become different within the two diagonal, and the two off-diagonal blocks, indicating that learning induces category-dependent structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2G and 2K.

claim: In some circuits, the category correlation becomes negative after learning.
source: In Figure 2G, the average correlation within the off-diagonal blocks is negative; the category correlation is thus negative (Cromer et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2010; Freedman and Miller, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2G and citations to experimental studies.

claim: Varying model details can switch the category correlation from negative to positive.
source: The model does not, however, always produce negative correlation: varying model details – either the parameters of the circuit or the number of stimuli – can switch the category correlation from negative to positive (Fitzgerald et al., 2013; one example is shown in Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2K and a citation to experimental work.

claim: When category correlation is negative, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have opposite sign.
source: In Figure 2H, where the category correlation is negative, the cloud has a negative slope. This is because changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have opposite sign: a neuron that increases its activity in response to category A decreases its activity in response to category B (Figure 2E left), and vice versa (Figure 2E right).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2H and 2E.

claim: When category correlation is positive, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have the same sign.
source: In Figure 2L, where the category correlation is positive, the cloud has, instead, a positive slope. Here, changes in single-neuron responses to categories A and B have the same sign: a neuron that increases its activity in response to category A also increases its activity in response to category B (Figure 2I, left), and similarly for a decrease (Figure 2I, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2L and 2I.

claim: In circuits with positive correlation, the number of neurons responding more strongly to category A is significantly larger than those responding more strongly to category B.
source: In Figure 2L, however, the number of neurons that respond more strongly to category A is significantly larger than the number of neurons that respond more strongly to category B (Fitzgerald et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 2L and a citation to experimental work.

claim: In circuits with positive correlation, the mean population activity in response to category A is larger than to category B.
source: Furthermore, as observed in experiments reporting positive correlations (Fitzgerald et al., 2013), the mean population activity in response to category A is larger than to category B, and the range of activity in response to A is larger than to B.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and a citation to experimental work.

claim: Over learning, all activity vectors acquire a component aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction.
source: Specifically, over learning all activity vectors acquire a component that is aligned with a common, stimulus-independent direction.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis presented in the paper.

claim: Over learning, activity vectors associated with different categories are pushed apart along the common direction d.
source: Consequently, over learning, activity vectors associated with different categories are pushed apart along d; this is illustrated in Figure 3B, C, which show activity for the two circuits analyzed in the second and third column of Figure 2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The increase in category selectivity is a robust byproduct of gradient-descent learning, observable in any circuit that learns the categorization task.
source: The generality of Equation 4 indicates that the increase in selectivity is a robust byproduct of gradient-descent learning, and so can be observed in any circuit that learns the categorization task, regardless of model details.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis showing the generality of the result.

claim: Category correlation depends on the threshold and gain of the readout neuron.
source: In Figure 4A, we show category correlation as a function of the threshold and gain of the readout neuron (Figure 1C). We find that varying those can change the magnitude and sign of correlations, with positive correlations favoured by large values of the threshold and gain and negative correlations favoured by small values.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Category correlation is affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer.
source: Category correlation is also affected by the threshold and gain of neurons in the intermediate layer. This can be seen in Figure 4B, which shows that larger values of the threshold and gain tend to favour positive correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Category correlation depends on multiple biophysical aspects of the circuit, which are likely to depend on brain areas.
source: Overall, these results indicate that category correlation depends on multiple biophysical aspects of the circuit, which in turn are likely to depend on brain areas.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of parameter dependencies.

claim: Correlation can vary across brain areas.
source: This suggests that correlation can vary across brain areas, which is in agreement with the observation that positive correlations reported in monkeys area LIP are robust across experiments (Fitzgerald et al., 2013), but inconsistent with the correlations observed in monkeys PFC (Cromer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Category correlation depends on the total number of stimuli.
source: Category correlation also depends on the total number of stimuli, a property of the task rather than the circuit (Materials and methods Simple task: category correlation, Equation 77).
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in correlation.
source: This is illustrated in Figure 4D, which shows that increasing the number of stimuli causes a systematic decrease in correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The model predicts that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
source: The model thus makes the experimentally testable prediction that increasing the number of stimuli should push category correlation from positive to negative values.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis.

claim: The magnitude of category selectivity for a given neuron depends on the magnitude of its initial connectivity with the readout neuron.
source: As a result, neurons with large initial connectivity develop large selectivity values (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The model predicts that changes in selectivity are determined by the strength of synaptic connections a neuron makes to downstream readout areas before learning.
source: In terms of biological circuits, Figure 5 predicts that changes in selectivity are determined by the strength of synaptic connections a neuron makes, before learning, to downstream readout areas.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis.

claim: Experiments in rodents PFC found that all neurons highly selective to a given abstract variable were characterized by similar downstream projections.
source: Experiments consistent with this prediction have been recently reported: studies in rodents PFC (Ye et al., 2016; Hirokawa et al., 2019) found that all neurons which were highly selective to a given abstract variable were characterized by similar downstream projections (i.e., they projected to the same area).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In the context-dependent task, each trial is specified by both a stimulus and a context cue.
source: On each trial, both a stimulus, and a context cue, are presented to the network.
evidence: This is a description of the task design.

claim: Before learning, initial category selectivity is weakly negative in the context-dependent task.
source: Before learning, activity is characterized by small selectivity, which is weakly negative on average (Figure 6A; the fact that average category selectivity is initially weakly negative is due to the composite nature of inputs for this task, see Materials and methods Detailed analysis of category selectivity).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6A and explained by the mathematical analysis.

claim: Over learning, the average category selectivity increases in the context-dependent task.
source: Over learning, the average category selectivity increases (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The average category selectivity increases in all circuit models in the context-dependent task, regardless of parameters.
source: As in the simple task, we found that the average category selectivity increases in all circuit models, regardless of the parameters (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Average context selectivity increases over learning in the context-dependent task.
source: We find, as we did for category selectivity, that average context selectivity increases over learning – a behaviour that is in agreement with experimental findings (Wallis et al., 2001; Stoet and Snyder, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and citations to experimental studies.

claim: The increase in context selectivity is highly robust and does not depend on model details.
source: The increase in context selectivity is, as for category, highly robust, and does not depend on model details (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic parameter variation shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The behavior of correlations is variable across circuits in the context-dependent task.
source: As in the simple task, the matrices acquire additional structure during learning, and that structure can vary significantly across circuits (Figure 6F, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6F and 6I.

claim: Context correlation can decrease or increase over learning depending on circuit parameters.
source: Context correlation behaves differently in the two circuits displayed in Figure 6F and I: it decreases over learning in Figure 6F, whereas it increases in Figure 6I.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6F and 6I.

claim: Over learning, activity vectors get re-arranged into statistically distinguishable clouds in the context-dependent task.
source: As in the simple task (Figure 3B, C), activity vectors get re-arranged into statistically distinguishable clouds.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: In the context-dependent task, four clouds are formed after learning, one for each combination of category and context.
source: While in the simple task clouds were determined by category, here each cloud is associated with a combination of category and context. As a result, four clouds are formed: the cloud of orange circles corresponds to category A and context 1; orange squares to category A and context 2; blue circles to category B and context 1; and blue squares to category B and context 2.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: The increase in clustering by category and context is independent of model parameters.
source: Mathematical analysis indicates that the increase in clustering by category and context is independent of model parameters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), which explains the robustness of the increase in selectivity observed in simulations.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis and supported by simulation data.

claim: The emergence of category-related structure is directly inherited from the readout neuron becoming category dependent.
source: The emergence of category-related structure is, perhaps, not surprising: over learning, the activity of the readout neuron becomes category dependent, as required by the task; such dependence is then directly inherited by the intermediate layer, where activity clusters by category.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics.

claim: The emergence of context-related structure is surprising since the readout neuron activity does not depend on context.
source: The emergence of context-related structure is, on the other hand, more surprising, since the activity of the readout neuron does not depend on context.
evidence: This is an observation about the model behavior.

claim: Context-dependent structure emerges as a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule.
source: Such novel structure is a signature of the gradient-descent learning rule used by the circuit (Canatar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to related work on gradient-descent learning.

claim: Context clustering emerges because how similarly intermediate-layer representations evolve is determined by both target category and correlations.
source: But, roughly speaking, context clustering emerges because, for a pair of sensory inputs, how similarly their intermediate-layer representations evolve during learning is determined both by their target category and their correlations (Equation 27, Materials and methods Evolution of connectivity and activity in large circuits).
evidence: This is an explanation derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The region of parameter space leading to an increase in correlation shrinks substantially in the context-dependent task compared to the simple task.
source: However, we find that the region of parameter space leading to an increase in correlation shrinks substantially compared to the simple task (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, see also Materials and methods Context-dependent task: computing activity); this is in line with the observation that correlations decrease to negative values when the complexity of the task increases, as shown in Figure 4D.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are, before learning, strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron.
source: As in the simple task, this leads to the prediction that neurons that strongly increase selectivity to either category or context are, before learning, strongly connected to the downstream readout neuron (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the mathematical analysis and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The model predicts that among strongly connected neurons, neurons with pure selectivity to category and neurons with mixed selectivity to category and context should be observed, but neurons with pure selectivity to context should not.
source: This makes the following experimental prediction: among all the neurons that are strongly connected to the readout, neurons with pure selectivity to category and neurons with mixed selectivity to category and context should be observed, but neurons with pure selectivity to context should not.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model analysis.

claim: The asymmetry between category and context arises because the readout neuron learns to read out category but not context.
source: The asymmetry between category and context arises because, in the model, the readout neuron learns to read out category, but not context.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model behavior.

claim: If a second readout neuron that learns to read out context is included, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
source: We show in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E, F that if a second readout neuron, which learns to read out context, is included in the circuit, neurons with strong pure selectivity to context are also observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E and 3F.

claim: Pure- and mixed-selective neurons are characterized by different properties of initial activity, specifically different initial patterns of response gain.
source: Analysis reported in Materials and methods Analysis of patterns of context and category selectivity indicates that these two populations are characterized by different properties of the initial activity. In particular, the two populations are characterized by different initial patterns of the response gain (defined as the slope of the activation function, Figure 1C, at the response), which measures the local sensitivity of neurons to their inputs.
evidence: This claim is derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Pure- and mixed-selective neurons can be distinguished based on their initial response gain patterns.
source: The fact that pure- and mixed-selective neurons can be distinguished based on these patterns is illustrated in Figure 8C.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: Initial activity, which is mostly unstructured and task-agnostic, plays an important role in learning by breaking symmetry among neurons and determining functional specialization.
source: Overall, these results indicate that initial activity, which is mostly unstructured and task-agnostic, plays an important role in learning: it breaks the symmetry among neurons in the intermediate layer, and determines which functional specialization neurons will display over learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of selectivity patterns.
